description: The image displays two side-by-side bar charts illustrating the relationship between Fleiss Kappa (a measure of inter-rater reliability) and two different ambiguity metrics: “Ambiguity Std” on the left and “Max Ambiguity” on the right. Both charts share the same vertical axis, labeled “Fleiss Kappa,” ranging from 0.0 to 0.8 in increments of 0.2, with values displayed above each bar. In the left chart, the horizontal axis is labeled “Ambiguity Std” and shows four categories: 0.0, 0.47, 0.82, and 0.94. The corresponding Fleiss Kappa values are 0.88, 0.46, 0.03, and 0.24, respectively, with bar heights decreasing then slightly increasing as ambiguity increases. The bars are colored in shades of blue, with the darkest bar at 0.0 and progressively lighter shades for higher ambiguity values. In the right chart, the horizontal axis is labeled “Max Ambiguity” with integer categories 1, 2, and 3. The Fleiss Kappa values are 0.89, 0.46, and 0.23, respectively, showing a clear decreasing trend as maximum ambiguity increases. The bars here are also shaded in progressively lighter blue tones. Both charts visually suggest that higher ambiguity correlates with lower agreement among raters, as measured by Fleiss Kappa, with the exception of the slight uptick at Ambiguity Std = 0.94. The charts appear to support findings from the paper “Defending Against Social Engineering Attacks in the Age of LLMs,” likely demonstrating how ambiguity in prompts or responses affects human annotator consistency — a critical factor in evaluating LLM-generated content for social engineering risks.
